extracted.intended_audience: General readers, journalists, legal scholars and policy watchers interested in presidential social media use, platform moderation, and related legal/political consequences
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing political/social-media content (especially presidential tweets) and platform responses — including categories of policy violations, legal/archival obligations, marketplace effects, and enforcement actions. Useful for analyzing moderation decisions, legal challenges, and public impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of unconstitutionally motivated animus
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may cite public statements by the President and advisers (including Tweets) as evidence that an action 'drips with religious intolerance, animus, and discrimination' or is unconstitutionally motivated (e.g., anti-Muslim animus in travel-ban litigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public statements, tweets, and other extrinsic communications can be used by challengers and courts to infer intent/motive; include both contemporaneous tweets and broader communication patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Announcement via Twitter undermines deliberative process
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden policy announcements made via Twitter without formality or deliberative processes can undermine governmental claims about motivations (Jane Doe v. Trump found an abrupt Twitter announcement bolstered plaintiffs' claim the policy was not driven by genuine concerns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a major policy is announced informally and without usual procedures, courts may view that as probative of improper motive or lack of legitimate justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on the stock market
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets by public figures can move stock prices and market capitalization (examples: Lockheed Martin, Boeing, Amazon, Goodyear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate temporal correlation between tweet and market reaction; note there are contrary examples where targeted negative tweets did not depress stock; examine market cap changes, rival gains, and corporate responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deletion of social media posts and Presidential Records Act compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Deletion of presidential tweets may constitute destruction of presidential records in violation of the Presidential Records Act; watchdog groups have sued arguing deleted tweets are federal records that must be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presidential and official social-media posts are generally considered presidential records; deletion-record retention practices can be legally challenged; National Archives guidance and litigation history are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic integrity policy: scrutiny of statements affecting democratic participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter's 'civic integrity' policy scrutinizes statements that may affect participation in democracy and invites nonprofits to flag problematic tweets in this area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform may proactively flag or act on posts that could mislead voters or affect civic processes; policy revisions expand scope over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-check advisories / 'Get the facts' labels for unsubstantiated claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter may place a fact-check advisory (e.g., 'Get the facts about mail-in ballots') on tweets alleging unsubstantiated claims, linking to explanatory or corrective information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when assertions (such as widespread mail-in ballot fraud) are unsubstantiated; labels aim to provide corrective context rather than remove content in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-interest exception for retaining world-leader content
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter has allowed a public-interest exception: it may choose to flag offensive tweets by current world leaders and candidates rather than remove them, because of their relevance to ongoing matters of public importance; when such persons leave office they may be treated as private citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms may balance public-interest value against rule violations; the exception is time- and status-dependent (in-office vs private citizen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Glorifying violence category / public-interest notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets judged to be 'glorifying violence' (e.g., 'when the looting starts, the shooting starts') can be given a 'public interest notice'—flagged but left visible because of newsworthiness and public relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms may weigh risk of harm vs public interest; other platforms may differ (e.g., Facebook opted not to act in similar cases), and such decisions draw journalistic and civil-rights scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulated media label
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that has been edited or presented in a misleading way (e.g., a satirical video altered with a network logo and false caption) may be labeled as 'manipulated media'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when media has been deceptively altered or context is false; label aims to warn viewers that the content does not represent authentic reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abusive behavior rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets that violate platform rules on abusive behavior (e.g., threats or language suggesting 'will be met with serious force') can receive warnings or strikes under abuse policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms may apply warnings, temporary locks, or removals depending on severity and context; similar language can trigger protective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading health-claims under civic-integrity (voter participation risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about health-related risks tied to civic processes (e.g., 'Mail Drop Boxes...are not Covid sanitized' implying voting by mail is unsafe) can be flagged under civic integrity for potentially dissuading participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess factual basis and potential to deter participation; labels may be applied where claims are unsupported and could suppress voting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading about an election / disputed election content
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets disputed or potentially misleading about elections or civic processes can be flagged as 'disputed' or 'misleading' (Twitter applied this to many tweets between election night and the victory speech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms may apply election-specific flags during sensitive periods but may adjust practices after results are settled; contextual timing matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content removal for copyright (DMCA) compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms will remove content in response to valid DMCA takedown requests (e.g., campaign video removed after DMCA request for an image used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyright law can compel removal regardless of political content; removal reasons should be transparent where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension for risk of further incitement of violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts can be permanently suspended when platform review concludes the account poses a 'risk of further incitement of violence' (Twitter cited this as the reason for permanently suspending @realDonaldTrump after Jan 6, 2021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms consider specific tweets, context, and indicators of real-world organization/proliferation of violence; temporary locks and removals may precede permanent bans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary locks and required deletions as stepped enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms may initially lock accounts (e.g., 12-hour locks) and require deletion of specific tweets as an intermediate enforcement step prior to suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement often follows an escalation path: warnings → locks → required deletions → suspensions; documentation of prior measures can justify later permanent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban-evasion and sock-puppet enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms enforce against ban evasion by detecting and permanently suspending sock-puppet accounts or attempts to repost content to evade bans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinstatement and evasion detection policies include permanent suspension 'at first detection' for evasion attempts tied to a banned user.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 230 and legal challenges to platform immunity/actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Moves to alter platform liability (e.g., executive orders targeting Section 230) implicate First Amendment and statutory limits; experts view many such measures as legally problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and constitutional constraints shape the range of permissible regulatory demands; platform actions can prompt litigation and Congressional scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archival and public-access obligations for presidential social-media
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative proposals and National Archives practices treat presidential social-media posts as records to be preserved and made publicly available (COVFEFE Act proposed; National Archives confirmed tweets are presidential records).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should identify official vs personal accounts, designate records, and ensure archival access; failure or delay in archiving can be contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and public reaction context as an evaluative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderator decisions and platform policies are evaluated against public reaction, partisan splits, foreign leader responses, and advocacy groups' positions (surveys showed divided public opinion on bans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider political polarization and international viewpoints when assessing the acceptability and impact of moderation actions; public reaction can influence corporate and regulatory responses.
